newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - July 1.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - July 1.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Hong Kong-based shipping firm Orient Overseas Container Line has opened talks with the New South Wales Government about building a A$140 million international container terminal at Sydney's Port Botany. The company originally wished to build the facility at the Port of Melbourne, but has been deterred by a range of commercial and legal objections to the project raised by the local community. Page 1.

The return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule has significant implications for the security status of the Asia-Pacific region as it raises the spectre of possible future confrontations with the US. Possible areas of dispute are China's reputed commitment to ganing control of democratic Taiwan, whose independence has been guaranteed by the US, and the preservation of civil liberties in Hong Kong. Page 1.

The role of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) in ensuring the deregulation of the telecommunications market results in a more efficient, competitive industry has been affirmed by the Federal Government. Federal Arts and Communicatons Minister Richard Alston said yesterday that the ACCC's management of access prices was pivotal to the emergence of "third-generation" competition. Page 1.

The textile, clothing and footwear industry has threatened to move offshore if the Federal Government implements the Industry Commission draft report's recommendation to cut industry protection levels to 5 per cent by 2008. The Council of Textile and Fashion Industries of Australia president Robert Hershan said yesterday that a move to single-digit tariff levels would result in the loss of 50,000 industry jobs. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Hong Kong reverted to Chinese sovereignty at midnight last night in a dramatic and moving ceremony. Former Governor Chris Patten and Prince Charles departed from Hong Kong immediately after the ceremony on the Royal Yacht Britannia, with their departure being preceded by the arrival of China's two most important leaders, President Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng. Page 1.

Tasmanian poet Peter Shoobridge, who murdered his four daughters and then committed suicide on the weekend, posted a total of 15 letters to family and friends before the event in an apparent farewell ritual. Tasmanian police have made public some of the details contained in the letters which indicate Shoobridge's disturbed state of mind. Page 3.

Fierce competition between telecommunications companies has already begun ahead of today's full deregulation of the industry. Australia's third largest phone company, AAPT, yesterday announced plans to drop its prices, thereby undercutting main rivals Testra and Optus by up to 60 per cent on international calls and 50 per cent on STD calls. Page 3.

Prime Minister John Howard has indicated to the textile, clothing and footwear industries that the Government will approve the Industry Commission's recommendation to reduce the sector's protection levels. Howard said yesterday that the TCF industries are unlikely to be offered a reprieve on tariffs like that offered to the car industry a month ago. Pate 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Chinese President Jiang Zemin ordered 4000 troops from the People's Liberation Army to enter Hong Kong immediately prior to the handover ceremony, disregarding a previous agreement which would have seen an advance party of 500 soldiers enter the territoryat 9pm today to prepare for a later, large-scale arrival of troops. The official New China News Agency indicated the move came in response to calls by world leaders for China to respect the democratic freedoms of its new territory. Page 1.

The Federal Government's lifting of restrictions on the setting up of non-Government schools has resulted in a major expansion of the private system nation-wide. New figures from the Federal Department of Education show that approvals for private school funding have doubled since last year leading to protests from the Australian Education Union and the NSW Teachers Federation. Page 1.

Tasmanian police are examining a sheaf of letters posted by Peter Shoobridge last Saturday before he murdered his four daughters Rebecca, 18, Anna, 14, Sara, 12, and Georgina, 9, and then committed suicide. Police hope the letters will clarify Shoobridge's motives, but Detective Sergeant Tony Bennett has commented that he "believes the motive will remain a mystery". Page 2.

Prime Minister John Howard visited New York's Yankee Stadium yesterday to express his support for Yankee relief pitcher Graeme Lloyd, an Australian who has successfully broken into the billion dollar American baseball industry. When in New York Howard also lobbied Wall Street to increase investment in the Australian economy. Page 2.
THE AGE

Federal Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer has stated that he trusts the Chinese Government to respect civil liberties in Hong Kong. Speaking after meeting his Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen in Hong Kong, Downer said that Australia would be gravey concerned if promises such as the guarantee of free and fair elections for a governing council were not met. Page A2.

Business leaders in the textile, clothing and footwear industries said yesterday they would consider moving production offshore if the Federal Government adopted the Industry Commission's proposals to slash their protection levels to 5 per cent by 2008. Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett has joined the industry in urging the Federal Government to reject the report's recommendations. Page A4.

Friends and neighbours have been stunned by the actions of Tasmanian poet Peter Shoobridge, who on Saturday murdered his four daughters before committing suicide. Investigations are focusing on a series of letters he posted and events sucs as his separation from his wife and employment difficulties. Page A5.

The Federal Court ruled yesterday that there were significant irregularities in the contract Airservices Australia awarded to American aerospace company Hughes to upgrade its air-traffic control network, saying it had breached the Trade Practices Act. Airservices Australia is now facing a giant damages payout to the American company. Page A6.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
